title: My Own Mayday
blurb: The first distress call comes in your own voice. It is dated three weeks from now, it names a nav beacon you have never visited, and it says pirates are waiting there. They are. Every call after it names another place and another date, always a little ahead of you, and something out in the dark is listening to the calls as well. The only way to make them stop is to follow them to the end.
inYourWords: I have a Sidewinder still in yard paint, a few hundred credits, and nobody to talk to but the ship. Then a mayday came in on a band nothing uses. The voice was mine. I have played it back a dozen times, and it is my voice, down to the way I say please. I never sent it, and the date on it hasn't happened yet.
beacon: Every call rides the carrier of a Guardian beacon. If a beacon is sending my voice, the beacon is where I find out how.

title: Ride Along
tone: Warm, wry road trip that turns tender
blurb: There is someone in your cargo hold. Juno Ashby says she flies search and rescue, that she lost her licence over a misunderstanding, and that she will earn her passage. She hears a distress call before your scanner does, and she is the best company you have had in years. She is also lying to you about something, and every pilot she sends you to save has heard her name before.
inYourWords: I bought the Sidewinder with everything I had, which was not much, and I liked flying it alone. Nobody to owe, nobody owing me. Then on my third jump the hold reported a mass it should not have, and the mass turned out to be a rescue pilot with a bag, a grin and no licence. She says she will pay her way. I have not decided yet whether to let her.
beacon: Juno's first payment is a tip: a Guardian beacon nobody has scanned, out past the last station she worked. The data should be worth something, and she says she knows the way.

title: Black Box
blurb: The yard sold you the cheapest Sidewinder on the lot, a rebuild with a clean title. They missed the flight recorder. Its last pilot went missing eleven months ago, and a well-dressed man named Selden Pryce will pay you on delivery to find out why. Every lead takes you somewhere new: a salvage field, a scrap yard, a distress call nobody answered. Every report you send him, he reads very carefully.
inYourWords: I bought the cheapest Sidewinder on the lot, with a clean title and a few hundred credits left over. The yard said it was wiped by the book. They missed the flight recorder. Every time I start the drive it plays the same four seconds: a woman's voice, calm, reading out a set of coordinates and her name. Ines Harrow. Nobody has seen her in eleven months.
beacon: The coordinates on the recorder are a Guardian beacon. It was the last place Ines Harrow logged before she went quiet, and the first place anyone looking for her would go.

title: The Borrowed Callsign
blurb: The registry gave your new Sidewinder a callsign off the recycling list: Lark. By the end of the day dock crews are waving you to the front of the queue, pirates are plotting routes around you, and a reporter has asked for your side of a battle you were nowhere near. Lark is the most famous pilot on the frontier. You have four hundred credits and have never won a fight. People keep calling for Lark anyway, and somebody has to answer.
inYourWords: I bought the cheapest Sidewinder in the yard, and the registry gave it a callsign off the recycling list. Lark. The clerk, Ruth Pask, read it back twice and went pale. Since then I have been given free fuel, two offers of marriage and one death threat. I have never won a fight in my life. I have decided not to mention that.
beacon: The last entry in Lark's public log is a data-link scan of a Guardian beacon. If people are going to call me Lark, I should know what Lark went out there for.

title: The Far Side
blurb: Nico answered your post on the jobs board with a terrible joke and a good offer: split the contracts, you fly the cargo in, Nico flies it out. Nico is funny, generous with advice, and always somewhere you have just missed. A year of shared jobs and late-night messages makes Nico the best friend you have out here. You have never seen Nico's face. Every message arrives nine hours after it was sent. And Nico describes stars you cannot find on any chart.
inYourWords: Nobody lends a Sidewinder pilot anything, not even company, so I posted on the jobs board for a partner. One reply came. Nico. Bad jokes, good maths, and a ship Nico will not describe. We split the work: I fly the cargo in and Nico flies it out. We have not met yet. We keep just missing each other.
beacon: Nico's messages reach me stamped with the routing code of a Guardian beacon, and they arrive full of crackle. Nico says a data-link scan of the beacon will clear the line. I would like to hear Nico properly.

title: Journeyman
blurb: The Companions of the Lane are older than the Pilots Federation, and their mark still opens doors a licence does not. To earn it, a journeyman walks the Circuit: nine masters scattered across the bubble, one for every craft a pilot can learn, and each one works you until the work is good before they mark your book. Hauling, mining, the hunt, charts, living things, passage, the ground, salvage and the forge. The masters are old, the guild house that sent you has not sent anyone in twenty years, and Mother Agathe, who keeps it, swears a strongbox opens for whoever comes home with a full book. Linus, the only other journeyman on the road, is always one master ahead of you, and has far too much money for someone sleeping in guild bunks. The book takes a year. You start with a Sidewinder.
inYourWords: I had a stock Sidewinder, a few hundred credits, and nowhere to sleep but the cockpit when I found the guild house: a common room, a row of empty bunks, and a board of names with most of them crossed out. Mother Agathe keeps it. She feeds anyone who works. She watched me work for a week, then put a book in my hands: a page for a Guardian beacon, a page for each of nine masters, and one for a masterwork. She says a strongbox opens for whoever fills it. I wrote my name inside the cover.
beacon: The first page of the book belongs to no master. It asks for the data from a Guardian beacon, the oldest machine anyone has found that still does its job. Mother Agathe says every journeyman starts there, to see how long good work outlasts the people who did it.

title: Good Standing
blurb: You have flown alone for years: a working ship, some engineering done, and savings that one bad week could take. Then Maren Holt watched you hold a line in a conflict zone after your wing ran, and offered to sponsor you into the Brightwater Mutual. Four hundred independent pilots, one share each, a fund for the bad weeks, and a wing that comes when you call. Augustin Pell, the last of the twelve who founded it, says the charter is one line long: the Mutual looks after its own. The pay is the best you have had, and it is the first place in years that feels like home. Every war the Mutual fights comes through one broker, and nobody on the council will say who the broker works for.
inYourWords: I have flown independent for six years. I have a ship I trust, some engineering done on it, and enough savings that one bad week would not finish me, though two might. Last month I held a line in a conflict zone after my wing ran, and the pilot who came back for me was Maren Holt of the Brightwater Mutual. She has offered to sponsor me. Four hundred pilots, one share each, a fund for the bad weeks, and a wing on call. Augustin Pell, who founded it, bought me a drink and told me the charter is one line. I have never belonged to anything. I have not said yes yet.
beacon: Every member of the Mutual flies the Founding Run before their first vote: a data-link scan of a Guardian beacon, as the founding twelve did the night they signed the charter. Maren says it is the only test the Mutual sets.

title: The Omphalos
blurb: You have a fleet carrier, a hangar of ships, and more credits than you will ever spend. There is very little left that money buys you. Then Hester Vane comes aboard: ninety years old, sixty of them spent hunting Raxxla, and the last living member of the Dark Wheel. She does not need your money or your guns. She needs your carrier and a year of your time, because the only real lead the Dark Wheel ever had is a Guardian star chart a million years old, and reading it will take the whole width of the galaxy. A salvage magnate with a carrier of his own has heard about the chart too, and he has never lost an auction.
inYourWords: I own a fleet carrier, a hangar of ships I rarely fly, and more credits than I can spend. Not much surprises me any more. Then an old explorer named Hester Vane docked at my carrier, asked for tea, and told me she was the last of the Dark Wheel. She has been looking for Raxxla for sixty years. She did not ask for money. She asked for my carrier, and for a year.
beacon: Hester says every Guardian beacon's data-link carries the same star chart, and that every member of the Dark Wheel scanned one and came away with something they could not read. She thinks it lists a world no human catalogue does. To read it, I need something aboard that reads Guardian charts, and she says the beacon is where I will find that too.

title: The Scholarship
blurb: You grew up in your parents' scrapyard, and the only person there who was ever kind to you was the engineer they hired. The engineer helped you build a Sidewinder out of scrap and fitted it with a transponder nobody can follow, and you ran. Months later, half-starved at the edge of the charts, a well-dressed man named Augustin Rell offers you a scholarship: training, a Pilots Federation combat certification, steady contracts, and a vitamin shot to put the weight back on. Since that shot you have not lost a fight. You have not backed away from one either.
inYourWords: I grew up in my parents' scrapyard, mostly in the way. The engineer they hired was the only one who ever asked whether I had eaten. The engineer helped me put a Sidewinder together out of three wrecks and fitted a transponder my parents can't follow. I left one night and didn't look back. That was months ago. I have the Sidewinder, a few hundred credits, and nobody who knows where I am.
beacon: The scholarship's first contract after certification: fly to a Guardian beacon, make a data-link scan, and bring the Lantern Fund everything it holds. Rell says the Fund collects them. The fee would feed me for a year.

title: The Hillside
tone: Relentless, tense, a siege against the clock
blurb: Three hundred and forty miners live at Ukah Mining Territory, on a grey moon in LHS 145, and they have seventy-two hours. The Kade Combine has ringed their system with interdictors and set the terms: leave the mine, or be there when the settlement's shield fails. They are not leaving. Their foreman is Tamsin Rook, who flew on your wing for six years and never asked you for anything. Last night she called, and she still did not ask. You have a fleet carrier, a hangar of ships and three days. Varro Kade has never lost a siege. And from the moment your carrier arrives, he stops caring about the mine.
inYourWords: I have a fleet carrier, more ships than I can fly in a month, and enough credits that nobody has been able to threaten me in years. Tamsin Rook flew on my wing for six years, then went off to dig rock on a moon in LHS 145 that nobody has heard of. Last night she called. The Kade Combine has blockaded her system, and her settlement's shield has three days of power left. She did not ask me to come. She said she only needed someone to know. I have already plotted the jump.
beacon: Rook says the Combine's trouble started far past the edge of the bubble, at a Guardian beacon where Kade has kept a ship parked for a year, listening. Before I go to her, I am going to scan that beacon and find out what he is listening for.

title: One Star
tone: Dry, quick comedy that turns warm
blurb: Horace Penhallow is the most feared critic in human space. One line in Penhallow's Starlanes once emptied a starport bar that had served drinks for two hundred years. Now he has booked a week aboard your fleet carrier for a new edition, and he has brought his own itinerary: ten sights, in order, starting with a Guardian beacon and including the longest supercruise in the bubble. Wynn Odoro, who runs your carrier's bar, says one star will empty it for a decade. You have flown through wars without blinking. You have never been reviewed. Penhallow writes down everything, including you, and he has not smiled once.
inYourWords: I have a fleet carrier, a hangar of ships and more credits than I can spend, and I have not taken a day off in years. There is always a jump to plot or a market to restock. Yesterday Wynn Odoro, who runs the bar on my carrier, came up to the bridge white as a sheet. Horace Penhallow has booked passage. The Horace Penhallow. He wants a week, a cabin with a view, and a tour of ten sights. Wynn says he reviews everything, the host included. I said I would fly him round for a week. How hard can it be?
beacon: Sight one on Penhallow's itinerary is a Guardian beacon, scanned by data-link with him watching from the jump seat. He says a review that starts anywhere else is a press release.

title: Runner-Up
blurb: For twenty years you have come second to Delphine Ashcroft. Second to Elite in trade. Second to the edge of the Formidine Rift. Second, by a few minutes, to the first data-link with the Guardian beacon in Synuefe KU-F b44-4, and the plaque at Lave Station still says so. Now Ashcroft is retiring, and she has called you to Lave for one last contest on the old terms: eleven days, three legs, and the loser says it out loud on the Lanes Report. First she asked you to fly back to that beacon and scan it again. She would not say why.
inYourWords: I have a fleet carrier, a hangar of engineered ships and more credits than I will ever spend, and there is one name I have never beaten. Delphine Ashcroft and I have raced each other for twenty years, and she has won every time, including the race that matters most to me: the first data-link with the Guardian beacon in Synuefe KU-F b44-4. Her name is on the plaque at Lave Station. Mine is under it. I have not been back to that beacon since. Last week she told me she is retiring, and challenged me to one more contest before she goes. I said yes before she finished the sentence.
beacon: Ashcroft asked me to go back to the beacon in Synuefe KU-F b44-4, where she beat me twenty years ago, and scan it again before I come to Lave Station. I have scanned it. Something happened that did not happen the first time.

title: The Milk Run
blurb: For fifty years Ida Vance has flown the same five stops in the same old Type-6: one refinery and four farms in LHS 2270, a system nobody visits. You left at seventeen and became a pilot the whole bubble knows. You have spoken to her ten times since. Now her heart is failing and she has a month. She has asked for one last run with you, and one detour first: the Guardian beacon where your father died before you were born. Your brother Tobias, who stayed, flies the second ship and has not forgiven you. Your mother keeps a paper ledger she will not let anyone read. You have a fleet carrier, a hangar of ships and more credits than you can spend, and none of it will buy her another month.
inYourWords: I left home at seventeen in a Sidewinder and did not look back. My mother, Ida, has flown the same five stops in LHS 2270 for fifty years: one refinery and four farms, the same faces every week, small cargo and smaller money. I needed more than that, and I got it: a fleet carrier, a hangar of engineered ships, and a name people know. We have spoken perhaps ten times in twenty years. Last night she sent word that her heart is failing and she has a month, and she asked me to fly the run with her one last time. My brother Tobias, who stayed, sent nothing.
beacon: My father, Cal Vance, died beside a Guardian beacon out past the edge of the bubble, a month before I was born. My mother has never seen the place. Before the run she has asked me to fly her there, and I am going to scan the beacon while she watches.

title: The Long Hour
tone: Quiet, haunted, a reckoning with your own record
blurb: Two years after the Thargoid war, the Joint Remembrance Board is giving you the highest citation it has. It is for the Long Hour, when an evacuation pilot held a lane open through a Thargoid swarm and eleven thousand people reached the jump point. The newsfeeds already carry your face, and in three months Commodore Lucan Strade will present the citation himself. There is one problem. You do not remember the hour. Twelve minutes without air in a breached cockpit took all of it, and your flight recorder came back blank. Rhea Calder flew on your wing that day. She will not come to the ceremony, and she has one thing to say about it: don't take it.
inYourWords: I flew evacuations through the whole war on a wing of three, callsign Ladder: Rhea Calder, Ansel Teague and me. Ansel didn't come home. Since the peace I've built up a fleet carrier, more ships than I can fly and more credits than I need, and mostly I haul cargo nobody is shooting at. Now the Remembrance Board says I held the lane at the Long Hour and saved eleven thousand people. I'd like to believe it. I don't remember a minute of it.
beacon: The citation says my hour was reconstructed from outside telemetry. An old anti-xeno hand at Veterans Retreat told me what that means: all through the war, the Guardian beacons were listening for Thargoids, and the Board pulled its record from them. If a beacon heard my hour, I'm going to hear it too.

title: Standing Order
tone: Generous, then uneasy, then quietly brave
blurb: You parked your fleet carrier over a mining outpost on the edge of the bubble for a week's refit. That afternoon raiders came for the outpost's ore, and you had them cleared before your coffee went cold. The miners threw you a party. Ada Corwen, who has run the outpost for thirty years, cried and pretended she had not. There is a great deal one pilot can fix with a carrier, a hangar of engineered ships and more credits than anyone needs, and for the first time in years somebody needs you. So you stay. Your ships fly the patrols, your carrier's market buys the ore, and the outpost has never been safer. Then Rennick Hale, who buys mining claims for a living, docks at the outpost, looks up at your carrier and asks how long you mean to stay.
inYourWords: I have a fleet carrier, a hangar of ships engineered as far as they go, and more credits than I will ever spend. Nobody has needed anything from me in years except a docking fee. Last week I parked the carrier over a mining outpost on the edge of the bubble for a refit, and that afternoon raiders came for the outpost's ore. I dealt with them before my coffee went cold. Ada Corwen, who runs the place, threw me a party in the ore hall and asked me to stay a little longer. I said a week. The week is up, and I have not plotted a jump.
beacon: The outpost's founders came out here thirty years ago following the signal of a Guardian beacon, and every pilot the outpost counts as its own has flown to a beacon and made a data-link scan of it. Ada has asked me to. Nobody has asked me to belong anywhere in a long time.

title: Next of Kin
tone: Warm, watchful, a found family on the run
blurb: For twenty years Vesna Kaul beat you to every contract worth having, and you never once caught her. Now she is dead, her ship lost on a quiet run, and her will names you, of all the pilots in the galaxy, guardian of a daughter you never knew she had. Linnet is fourteen, furious, and a better natural pilot than anyone on your carrier. She hums in her sleep, the same few notes every night. She has never seen a Guardian beacon. Dr. Corin Wexley, the soft-spoken scientist who paid for her mother's last survey, has asked to meet her. Vesna's will has one more line, underlined twice: never let him.
inYourWords: I have a fleet carrier, a hangar of ships and more credits than I will ever spend. For twenty years there was one pilot I could never beat, Vesna Kaul, and I think she was half the reason I kept flying. Last week a Pilots Federation clerk told me she was dead, and that her will names me guardian of her daughter. I did not know she had one. Linnet came aboard this morning with one bag, walked past me without a word, and chose the cabin furthest from mine. The carrier has never been this quiet.
beacon: Linnet hums the same few notes in her sleep, and has all her life. The carrier's comms log matches them to the carrier signal of a Guardian beacon. She has never seen one, and for the first time since she came aboard, she has asked me for something.

title: Honest Work
blurb: You are a good pilot and better company, and you have not told the whole truth in years. The cargo was late because of pirates. You visit your father often. And for sixteen years Bram Tolliver, eighty next month and the proudest old man at Hutton Orbital, has believed his child is a lieutenant in the Federal Navy, because that is what your letters say. For his birthday he has asked for one thing: a picture of his lieutenant beside a Guardian beacon, lit. You fly out to take it, and you scan the beacon so it lights for the camera. What comes aboard with the scan cannot abide a false record, and from then on every message your ship sends goes out with a correction attached. Your sister Hanne has questions. So does everyone else.
inYourWords: I fly freight and the odd charter in a ship I have put real money into, engineering and all, and I have enough saved that a bad month would not sink me. I am good at the work and better at the talking. When a cargo is late, it was pirates. When my sister Hanne asks, I visit Dad often. My father, Bram, flew Eagles off a Federal Navy carrier for thirty years, and I applied to the Navy flight academy because of him. I washed out at nineteen. I never told him. I wrote to him as a lieutenant instead, and I have been writing ever since. He turns eighty next month at Hutton Orbital, and he has asked for a picture of me at a Guardian beacon, because my last letter said I was posted to a Navy survey of Guardian sites. I am going to get him one.
beacon: My letters say I am posted to a Navy survey of Guardian sites. For his eightieth birthday my father has asked for a picture of his lieutenant beside a Guardian beacon, lit up. A beacon only lights for a data-link scan, so I am going to scan one and take the picture.

title: Dark Horse
tone: Brisk, sly comedy that turns earnest
blurb: Every pilot at Ray Gateway knows your name, and none of them takes you seriously. You are the one at the end of the bar who says the Guardian beacons answer back if you scan them properly, and last month Moss Varley, who runs the bar, opened a book on it. So you flew out and scanned one. While you were gone, somebody put your name on the ballot for Pilots' Steward, the seat on the station board that sets the docking levy and runs the rescue fund. Imogen Thale has held it for fourteen years. The vote is in eleven days, the station newsfeed calls you the joke candidate, and Moss has already had the badges made.
inYourWords: I fly a working ship out of Ray Gateway in Diaguandri. I have done some engineering on it, I have savings enough for a bad month, and I have a seat at the end of the pilots' bar that everybody knows is mine. I also have a theory: that the Guardian beacons answer back if you scan them properly. Nobody at the bar believes it. Last month Moss Varley opened a book on it at eleven to one, and I flew out to settle the matter. On the way home the newsfeed told me my name is on the ballot for Pilots' Steward, against Imogen Thale, who has held the seat for fourteen years. I did not put it there. Moss says he has no idea who did, and he has already had badges made.
beacon: Moss Varley opened a book at the bar on whether a Guardian beacon answers back when it is scanned properly, at eleven to one against. I flew out to the beacon to settle it, and I have scanned it. I am not saying yet who won the book.

title: Point of Order
tone: Dry parliamentary comedy that turns earnest
blurb: The Ice is two frozen worlds at the edge of Eranin, four thousand miners and one seat on the Eranin Assembly. The only candidate for it was the Speaker's nephew, until you filed against him in a bar, on a bet, with a platform one line long. Four percent of the Ice voted. You won by eleven. You have never read a law, you live in your cockpit, and Dee Mwangi, the refinery foreman, has called you a joke to your face. Speaker Barnaby Quell welcomes you warmly and puts you on a committee that has not met in forty years. Perpetua Gilchrist, Clerk of the Assembly for forty-one years, hands you the rules, all eleven hundred of them. Somebody aboard is going to read every one.
inYourWords: I have a working ship, some engineering done and savings that one bad month could take. I haul ore for the miners on the Ice, out at the edge of Eranin, and every time I dock I watch the Assembly's freight levy come off their pay. When the Ice's seat came up, the only candidate was the Speaker's nephew. I filed against him in a bar in Azeban City, on a bet, with one line: scrap the levy. I won by eleven votes. I am now the Member for the Ice. I have never read a law in my life, and I have just been handed eleven hundred of them.
beacon: Speaker Quell put me on the Committee on Xeno-Antiquities. It has not met in forty years and has one item outstanding: a survey of a Guardian beacon that the Assembly paid for and never received. The Clerk says a member who sits on a committee does its work. So I am going to fly out and scan it.
